lead: Compression rewrites data in fewer bits by removing redundancy. Redundancy is repeated or predictable information: repeated pixels, repeated frames, uneven symbol frequencies, or detail the eye ignores. Lossless compression reconstructs the exact original bytes. Lossy compression discards some detail, so the original cannot be recovered exactly. Every image, song and video on a phone uses these ideas. A photo gallery, a UPI receipt PDF and a video call all depend on compression to fit storage and network limits. This chapter defines redundancy, compression ratio and the main lossless and lossy methods.
prereq: You need: data sizes from Chapter 4.2 and file formats from Chapter 4.4 and Chapter 4.5.

blocks.text: Compression is the process of reducing the number of bits used to store or transmit data. Decompression reverses it. The need is simple: a 12-megapixel colour photo has about 36 million bytes of raw pixel data, too large for a chat app to send quickly. Compression works by finding redundancy.

Redundancy is data that can be predicted from other data. Four kinds matter. Spatial redundancy: neighbouring pixels in an image are often similar, as in a clear sky. Temporal redundancy: successive video frames are similar, as in a static cricket pitch. Coding redundancy: some symbols occur more often than others, so fixed-length codes waste bits. Psychovisual redundancy: the eye and ear ignore some detail, such as very fine texture or a quiet tone next to a loud one.
compression ratio = original size ÷ compressed size
blocks.where: original size is bits before compression; compressed size is bits after compression. Ratio above 1 means the compressed file is smaller.
original size and compressed size use the same unit. A file of 1000 bytes compressed to 250 bytes has ratio 4 and saving 75%.

sections.h3: Lossless methods: RLE, Huffman and LZW

blocks.text: Lossless compression reconstructs the exact original data. It is used when a changed byte matters: text files, source code, bank statements, medical scans, ZIP archives. Three classic methods appear in syllabi.

Run-length encoding (RLE) replaces a run of the same value by one value and a count. The string AAAABBBCCDAA becomes 4A3B2C1D2A. RLE is simple and fast. It works well on images with large flat areas, such as a cartoon or a scanned document. It can expand data when runs are short.

Huffman coding assigns short codes to frequent symbols and long codes to rare symbols. It builds a binary tree by repeatedly combining the two smallest weights. The code must be prefix-free: no code is the start of another code. This lets the decoder read bits left to right without separators. A fixed 3-bit code for six symbols always uses 3 bits per symbol. Huffman uses fewer bits on average when frequencies are uneven. The worked example below shows the calculation.

LZW (Lempel–Ziv–Welch) builds a dictionary of repeated strings while reading the data. It starts with single characters. When a string repeats, LZW adds it to the dictionary and later sends the dictionary index instead of the string. The decoder rebuilds the same dictionary, so no dictionary needs to be stored. LZW is used in GIF images and in some document formats. It is good at repeated words and patterns.

All three methods are lossless. Entropy coding is the general name for Huffman, arithmetic coding and similar final stages that pack symbols into bits. In a lossy pipeline, entropy coding is still the last lossless step.

sections.h3: Lossy methods: quantization, DCT and perceptual coding

blocks.text: Lossy compression discards detail that is less important to human perception. It cannot reconstruct the exact original. Some syllabi call it irreversible compression. It is used for photos, music and video, where a small loss is acceptable and the saving is large.

Quantization reduces the precision of numbers. A value 137 can be stored as 136 or 144 if the step size is 8. The decoder gets an approximation. Quantization is the main lossy step in image and audio codecs. A larger step gives a smaller file and more visible or audible error.

The discrete cosine transform (DCT) converts a block of pixels into frequency coefficients. Low-frequency coefficients describe broad shapes and smooth colour; high-frequency coefficients describe fine detail and edges. The codec quantizes high-frequency coefficients more coarsely because the eye notices them less. The inverse DCT rebuilds an approximate block. This is why JPEG can shrink a photo while keeping it recognisable. Details of the JPEG pipeline belong to Chapter 4.7.

Perceptual coding uses a model of hearing or vision. In audio, a loud tone masks a nearby quiet tone; the quiet tone can be removed without being heard. In video, the eye is less sensitive to fine colour detail than to brightness. The codec spends fewer bits on masked or less visible components. This is the basis of MP3 and AAC audio, and of video codecs.

After quantization, the remaining symbols are often entropy-coded with Huffman or arithmetic coding. That last stage is lossless; the loss already happened in quantization. Standards for MPEG audio and video are in Chapter 4.8.

figure.caption: The Huffman tree for A:45, B:13, C:12, D:16, E:9, F:5, built by merging the two smallest weights each time. Read each code off the 0/1 path from the root: the frequent A needs 1 bit, the rare F and E need 4 bits, so 100 symbols cost 224 bits instead of 300 for a fixed 3-bit code.

spec.aria: A Huffman tree for the frequencies A 45, B 13, C 12, D 16, E 9, F 5: merges give 14, 25, 30, 55 and root 100, and with 0 on left edges and 1 on right edges the codes are A=0, C=100, B=101, F=1100, E=1101, D=111.

examples.question: Huffman-code the six symbols with frequencies A:45, B:13, C:12, D:16, E:9, F:5. Give one valid prefix-free code, the average code length, and compare the total bits with a fixed 3-bit code for 100 symbols. Find the compression ratio and saving percentage.
steps: Sort weights ascending: F 5, E 9, C 12, B 13, D 16, A 45.
Merge the two smallest: F 5 + E 9 = N1 14.
Remaining: C 12, B 13, N1 14, D 16, A 45. Merge C 12 + B 13 = N2 25.
Remaining: N1 14, D 16, N2 25, A 45. Merge N1 14 + D 16 = N3 30.
Remaining: N2 25, N3 30, A 45. Merge N2 25 + N3 30 = N4 55.
Assign 0 to each left child and 1 to each right child. One valid code: A = 0, B = 101, C = 100, D = 111, E = 1101, F = 1100.
Code lengths: A 1 bit, B 3 bits, C 3 bits, D 3 bits, E 4 bits, F 4 bits.
examples.answer: The Huffman code has average length 2.24 bits/symbol, total 224 bits against 300 bits for the fixed code, compression ratio about 1.34 and saving about 25.3%.
examples.check:
weights = {'A':45,'B':13,'C':12,'D':16,'E':9,'F':5}
lengths = {'A':1,'B':3,'C':3,'D':3,'E':4,'F':4}
compressed = sum(weights[s]*lengths[s] for s in weights)
total = sum(weights.values())
avg = compressed/total
fixed = total*3
ratio = fixed/compressed
saving = (fixed-compressed)/fixed*100
print(round(avg,2))
print(compressed)
print(fixed)
print(round(ratio,2))
print(round(saving,1))

traps: A Huffman code must be prefix-free. If one code is the start of another, the decoder cannot split the bit stream.
A compression ratio above 1 means the compressed file is smaller. A ratio below 1 means the 'compressed' file is larger than the original.
Lossy compression cannot recover the exact original. Do not call it lossless even if the output looks or sounds the same.
In a lossy codec, entropy coding is lossless. The loss comes from quantization, not from Huffman coding.
Saving percentage uses the original size in the denominator, not the compressed size.

quiz.a: Lossless compression reconstructs the exact original data. Lossy compression discards some detail and cannot reconstruct the exact original.

quiz.q: Why must a Huffman code be prefix-free?
quiz.a: The decoder reads bits one after another without separators. If one code were the start of another, the same bit stream could be split in two ways, so decoding would be ambiguous.

quiz.q: Encode the string AAAABBBCCDAA with run-length encoding.
quiz.a: 4A3B2C1D2A. Four A, three B, two C, one D, two A.

quiz.q: A file of 800 KB is compressed to 200 KB. Find the compression ratio and saving percentage.
A lossy audio codec uses quantization followed by Huffman coding. Which step loses information, and why is the Huffman step still called lossless?
quiz.a: Quantization loses information by reducing precision. Huffman coding only packs the quantized symbols into bits and reconstructs those same symbols exactly, so it is lossless. The overall codec is lossy because of quantization.

quiz.q: Name the redundancy type: (a) repeated sky pixels in an image, (b) repeated frames in a video call, (c) letter e more frequent than z, (d) a quiet tone masked by a loud tone.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems use arithmetic coding, range coding and dictionary methods such as Brotli and Zstandard, which combine string matching with entropy coding. Neural compression uses learned models to predict pixels or audio samples and is an active research area. Search for 'rate-distortion theory', 'arithmetic coding' and 'perceptual audio coding' to go deeper. Information theory gives the entropy bound on lossless compression.
